clue.text: But fretwork needn't make one so

definitions.text: But fretwork needn't make one so

parts.words: But fretwork needn't make one so
parts.note: fretwork is a craft hobby, but read as the 'work' of fretting, worrying, it is what makes a person short-tempered

explanation.surface: A remark that a fretwork hobby need not make anyone irritable.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue plays on 'fret': the carpenter's fretwork versus fretting, worrying, which leaves one irritable.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who frets becomes irritable and quick to snap, which is the sense of the word.

clue.text: Does it create a precedent for action by the MCC ?

definitions.text: Does it create a precedent for action by the MCC ?

parts.words: Does it create a precedent for action by the MCC ?
parts.note: a legal action that settles a principle is read as a cricket matter for the MCC, the club once governing English cricket and its Test matches

explanation.surface: A question about whether cricket's governing club is setting a precedent.
explanation.walkthrough: The MCC (Marylebone Cricket Club) long ran English cricket; a Test is an international cricket match, so a legal 'case' about a Test is the cricketing reading.
explanation.definitionFit: A lawsuit brought to establish a legal principle for later disputes is called this.

clue.text: But at the cinema it comes before, not after

definitions.text: But at the cinema it comes before, not after

parts.words: But at the cinema it comes before, not after
parts.note: a vehicle towed behind something comes after it, yet the film preview of that name is shown before the main feature

explanation.surface: An observation about what is shown ahead of the main film.
explanation.walkthrough: A towed wagon trails behind; the film advertisement of the same name is screened ahead of the feature.
explanation.definitionFit: A short preview advertising a forthcoming film, screened before the main picture.

clue.text: You get little change where these are concerned

definitions.text: You get little change where these are concerned

parts.words: You get little change where these are concerned
parts.note: 'little change' reads as not much difference, but literally means small coins of slight value

explanation.surface: A grumble that things never really change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little change' means coins of tiny value; the old British halfpenny was worth half a penny.
explanation.definitionFit: Old British coins each worth half a penny, very small change indeed.

clue.text: Disingenuously Janus-like

parts.note: the Roman god Janus had two faces looking opposite ways, and an insincere person is said to have the same feature

explanation.surface: A description of someone insincere, likened to the two-headed Roman god.
explanation.walkthrough: Janus, Roman god of doorways, is pictured with two faces; in a deceitful sense the same description means hypocritical.
explanation.definitionFit: Hypocritical people show one look to you and another behind your back, like a god with a pair of heads.

clue.text: Crews eat course for change with relish

indicators.note: the letters are put up for change, so they are rearranged into a new order

explanation.surface: A rowing crew swaps one course of a meal for something tastier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for change' rearranges CREWS EAT COURSE into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A spicy condiment made in Worcester, a relish poured over food.

clue.text: What Oliver was; but not literally, in the workhouse

definitions.text: What Oliver was; but not literally, in the workhouse

parts.words: What Oliver was; but not literally, in the workhouse
parts.note: Dickens's Oliver Twist was starved in the workhouse, so he was weary of it but not, taken literally, well nourished

explanation.surface: A remark on the famished orphan of Dickens's novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliver Twist asked for more gruel; he was thoroughly sick of the workhouse, though literally never given enough food.
explanation.definitionFit: Being sick and tired of something; literally, having eaten well.

clue.text: Headgear said to suit French smokers

parts.note: a cap is a piece of headgear
something said is spoken, oral

explanation.surface: A hat thought suitable for French people who smoke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to suit' is a link. Caporal is a strong French tobacco, a cheap cigarette brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Caporal is a dark French tobacco, the stuff smoked in many French cigarettes.

clue.text: Hate to remove 1 dn's first half?

definitions.meaning: the first half of 1 down's answer is TEST

explanation.walkthrough: Read as DE-TEST, the word means removing the first four letters of 1 down.
explanation.definitionFit: To loathe intensely; read as de- plus a word, also taking away a trial.

clue.text: It should cause no difficulty to a make-up specialist

definitions.text: It should cause no difficulty to a make-up specialist

parts.words: It should cause no difficulty to a make-up specialist
parts.note: a make-up specialist sounds like a cosmetics artist, but read as one skilled at making up after quarrels

explanation.surface: A remark on a task easy for a theatrical cosmetics artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make-up' suggests cosmetics; to make up is to settle a quarrel.
explanation.definitionFit: Settling a quarrel and restoring friendship is making up.

clue.text: Does produce them, though they don't amount to much

definitions.text: Does produce them, though they don't amount to much

parts.words: Does produce them, though they don't amount to much
parts.note: does are female deer, which give birth to fawns; the young are animals of little size

explanation.surface: A comment that something gets done but yields little.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Does' looks like the verb but is the plural of doe, a female deer.
explanation.definitionFit: Young fawns are little animals of the antlered family, which does bear.

clue.text: A store of French cannabis

parts.note: de is French for 'of'
pot is slang for cannabis

explanation.surface: A stash of French drugs.
explanation.definitionFit: A warehouse or storehouse for goods is called this.

clue.text: Did she entertain Odysseus in song ?

definitions.meaning: the nymph who kept Odysseus on her island for seven years in Homer
a Caribbean ballad style from Trinidad

explanation.surface: A question whether a singer amused the Greek hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The Homeric nymph who detained Odysseus shares her name with a West Indian song form.

clue.text: Witnesses who, according to the Latin tag, should be believed ?

definitions.text: Witnesses who, according to the Latin tag, should be believed ?

parts.words: Witnesses who, according to the Latin tag, should be believed ?
parts.note: the Latin tag 'experto credite' means believe one who has experience; in court, specialists give testimony

explanation.surface: A question about which witnesses an old Latin saying trusts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Latin saying 'experto credite' (Virgil) tells us to trust those with experience; specialist witnesses give such evidence in court.
explanation.definitionFit: Specialist witnesses called for their knowledge, trusted on Virgil's advice.

clue.text: It is among the passerine birds

definitions.text: It is among the passerine birds

indicators.note: the letters sit among those of the following word, so the answer is found inside it

explanation.surface: A naturalist's statement placing a bird in the perching order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' points inside 'passerine'; and the bird found is itself a small finch, one of the passerines.
explanation.definitionFit: A small yellow European finch, which belongs to the perching order of birds.

clue.text: Used by old investors, if not glasshouse inmates

definitions.text: Used by old investors, if not glasshouse inmates

parts.words: Used by old investors, if not glasshouse inmates
parts.note: investors here are besiegers investing a town with ancient siege engines; people in glass houses should not throw stones

explanation.surface: A remark about tools of the financial world, unsuited to prisoners.
explanation.walkthrough: To invest a town is to besiege it; 'glasshouse' recalls the proverb that those in glass houses shouldn't throw stones (glasshouse is also British military slang for prison).
explanation.definitionFit: A siege engine for hurling stones, or a boy's forked sling.

clue.text: Fragrant musical medley

parts.note: the word names both a mixture of dried scented petals and a medley of tunes

explanation.surface: A sweet-smelling mix of tunes.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowl of scented dried petals; also a miscellany of musical pieces.

clue.text: Refrains as ordered by 28 ?

parts.note: 28 across, read as a double command to sing, is an order for repeated singing together

explanation.surface: Song refrains directed by the clue numbered 28.
explanation.walkthrough: 28 across, the prison, splits into 'Sing, sing!', an instruction to join in the refrains.
explanation.definitionFit: Repeated sections of a song sung by everyone together.

clue.text: One active on feast-days?

parts.note: a person busy celebrating at festivals and making merry

explanation.surface: A question about someone busy during religious holidays.
explanation.definitionFit: A merrymaker taking part in festivities.

clue.text: Formation of military strength step by step

definitions.text: Formation of military strength step by step

parts.words: Formation of military strength step by step
parts.note: a military arrangement of troops or aircraft placed in staggered steps

explanation.surface: Building up an army gradually.
explanation.definitionFit: A staggered formation in which each unit is set back from the one ahead, like a stair.

clue.text: What a cut-purse would have got from Iago

definitions.text: What a cut-purse would have got from Iago

parts.words: What a cut-purse would have got from Iago
parts.note: Iago says in Othello 'Who steals my purse steals' something worthless

explanation.surface: Wondering what a pickpocket would take from Shakespeare's villain.
explanation.walkthrough: Iago's line in Othello: 'Who steals my purse steals trash'. A cut-purse is an old word for a pickpocket.
explanation.definitionFit: Rubbish, the worthless stuff Iago claims his purse holds.

clue.text: The loan is arranged in Eire

indicators.note: the letters are arranged afresh, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A loan being set up in Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is arranged' rearranges THE LOAN; the definition is merely 'in Eire', a place there.
explanation.definitionFit: A town on the Shannon in the Irish republic.

clue.text: Caliban said the isle was full of them

definitions.text: Caliban said the isle was full of them

parts.words: Caliban said the isle was full of them
parts.note: Caliban in The Tempest tells his companions not to fear, for the island is full of sounds

explanation.surface: A recollection of a line from Shakespeare's Tempest.
explanation.walkthrough: Caliban's speech in The Tempest: 'Be not afeard, the isle is full of noises'.
explanation.definitionFit: Sounds and din, which Caliban says fill Prospero's island.

clue.text: ' Of ladies most deject and wretched "

definitions.text: ' Of ladies most deject and wretched "

parts.words: ' Of ladies most deject and wretched "
parts.note: a line Shakespeare gives to Polonius's daughter in Hamlet, describing herself

explanation.surface: A quotation lamenting a most miserable lady.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet, Act 3: 'And I, of ladies most deject and wretched' is spoken by Polonius's daughter after Hamlet rejects her.
explanation.definitionFit: Polonius's daughter in Hamlet speaks this line of herself.

clue.text: Connexions used by clubmen

definitions.meaning: golfers carrying clubs play on a seaside golf course

explanation.surface: Links of acquaintance exploited by members of a club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'clubmen' suggests members of a gentlemen's club; here they are golfers.
explanation.definitionFit: Joins in a chain, and a seaside golf course used by golfers.

clue.text: One more metamorphosis on earth

indicators.note: a metamorphosis is a change of form, so the letters change their arrangement

explanation.surface: Yet another transformation in the world.
explanation.walkthrough: 'metamorphosis' rearranges ON EARTH.
explanation.definitionFit: An additional one, a further example.

clue.text: Sage is shortly to take in a pupil

indicators.note: one word takes the other inside it, signalling a container

parts.note: shortly means soon
L, for learner, stands for a pupil

explanation.surface: A wise man is about to enrol a student.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is' is a link; L (learner, as on learner-driver plates) goes inside SOON.
explanation.definitionFit: Solon was the ancient Athenian lawgiver, and his name now means a wise statesman.

clue.text: Contract debts by not being inquisitive?

parts.note: to contract a debt is to incur it
IOUs are written promises of debts

explanation.surface: Running up debts by never asking questions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' is a link; IOUS are notes acknowledging debts.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking curiosity, showing no wish to know.

clue.text: Where jail-birds sound happy, it seems

definitions.text: Where jail-birds sound happy, it seems

parts.words: Where jail-birds sound happy, it seems
parts.note: the famous New York State prison has a name that sounds like a cheerful double command to sing

explanation.surface: A place where the prisoners seem to be singing for joy.
explanation.walkthrough: The prison at Ossining, New York, bears a name that sounds like birds singing.
explanation.definitionFit: A notorious maximum-security penitentiary on the Hudson in New York.

clue.text: Performers at a smoking concert?

parts.note: a smoking concert was an old men-only musical evening, but here the performers are those who smoke tobacco through a bowl and stem

explanation.surface: A question about the entertainers at a Victorian men's music night.
explanation.walkthrough: A 'smoking concert' was an informal men's musical evening; musicians who play bagpipes share a name with pipe smokers.
explanation.definitionFit: Musicians who play the pipes, especially bagpipes.
